title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the grammar of who does what

questions.prompt: An adviser gives a parent one piece of advice in two parts: the condition, "Trust your children", and the result, "They respect and appreciate you". Which single sentence joins them as an automatic result?

options.text: If you will trust your children, they respect and appreciate you.
If you trust your children, they are respecting and appreciating you.
If you trusted your children, they respect and appreciate you.
If you trust your children, they respect and appreciate you.

questions.explanation: An automatic result keeps a present tense in both halves, so the two orders become "If you trust your children, they respect and appreciate you." "If you will trust your children, they respect and appreciate you." puts will inside the if-clause, which English never allows, however future the advice sounds. "If you trust your children, they are respecting and appreciating you." swaps the simple present of a general rule for a continuous form, which describes one moment in progress instead. "If you trusted your children, they respect and appreciate you." leaves a past form in the first half beside a present in the second, so the two halves no longer match.

questions.prompt: Leila is taking part in a radio programme about family life. A listener has just finished saying that keeping the house tidy is the mother's job alone. Leila disagrees, but she is on the air and wants to stay courteous. Which reply does she choose?

options.text: You have a point, but the house belongs to all of us.
Oh no, that is completely wrong, and you know it perfectly well.
I am really exhausted and nobody in this house ever helps me.
Before you go on, let me finish my last sentence.

questions.explanation: Polite disagreement has two moves — grant the other speaker something, then object — and "You have a point, but the house belongs to all of us." makes both. "Oh no, that is completely wrong, and you know it perfectly well." does object, but it grants nothing and turns on the listener, so it fails the courtesy Leila is aiming for. "I am really exhausted and nobody in this house ever helps me." is a complaint about her own situation and answers nothing that the listener claimed. "Before you go on, let me finish my last sentence." is the phrase for interrupting a speaker who is still talking, and this listener has already finished.

questions.prompt: Read this note. "Mrs Ben Salah runs a small guest house. She never touches the sheets herself: every Friday two students come in, change them all, and she pays them for the work." Which sentence describes the arrangement?

options.text: She makes the two students change the sheets.
She lets the two students change the sheets.
She has the two students change the sheets.
She wants the two students change the sheets.

questions.explanation: The causative have is the verb for arranging a job that somebody else carries out for you, which is exactly what a paid Friday round is: "She has the two students change the sheets." "She makes the two students change the sheets." says she forces them, and nothing in the note forces anybody: they are paid. "She lets the two students change the sheets." says she merely gives permission, as if the work were theirs and the favour hers, when the work is hers and she buys it. "She wants the two students change the sheets." mixes the two structures: want always keeps its to, so it could only be wants them to change.

questions.prompt: A magazine article about the generation gap needs one word in each gap: "Teenagers complain that their parents are ___ , and parents answer that teenagers are ___ ." The two words are built on "patient" and on "grateful", each with the prefix that reverses it. Which pair fits?

options.text: unpatient / ingrateful
impatient / ungrateful
impatient / ingrateful
unpatient / ungrateful

questions.explanation: English reverses patient with im- and grateful with un-, so the pair is "impatient / ungrateful". "unpatient / ungrateful" gets the second word right and the first wrong, because no English word un-patient exists. "impatient / ingrateful" gets the first word right and the second wrong, because in- never attaches to grateful. "unpatient / ingrateful" is wrong on both counts. The reversing prefix follows no rule you can work out from the sound: it is learnt with its word, one pair at a time.

questions.prompt: Read what Hichem says, then complete the line "Areas of misunderstanding" of his file. "I get on well with my father about school; he even defends my marks in front of my uncles. What we never agree on is the evening: he wants me home at nine, and my friends stay out until eleven. My mother is fine about the time, but she opens my school bag every night and reads whatever is inside." Which line is right?

options.text: school marks; coming home late
privacy; school marks
pocket money; coming home late
coming home late; privacy

questions.explanation: Hichem names exactly two quarrels, the hour he must be home and his mother reading what is in his bag, so the line reads "coming home late; privacy". "school marks; coming home late" adds the marks, and the marks are the one subject on which he says his father takes his side. "privacy; school marks" repeats that same mistake with the two items in the other order. "pocket money; coming home late" invents money, which the text never mentions. A file line reports only what the speaker actually says, never what a reader expects a teenager to say.

questions.prompt: Two sentences describe the same mother: (1) "She has the girls clear the table." (2) "She has cleared the table." Who clears the table in each one?

options.text: The girls in the first, the mother in the second.
The mother in both, because both sentences use has.
The girls in both, because has always points to somebody else.
The mother in the first, the girls in the second.

questions.explanation: The first sentence is the causative: has is followed by an object, the girls, and then by the bare form clear, so the girls do the work and the mother only arranges it. The second is a perfect tense, has + the past participle cleared with nothing in between, so the mother did it herself. "The mother in both, because both sentences use has" trusts the word has alone, but a perfect tense never puts an object between the auxiliary and the verb, which the first sentence does. "The girls in both, because has always points to somebody else" turns one use of has into a rule; in the second sentence has is simply the auxiliary. "The mother in the first, the girls in the second" reverses the two structures exactly.
